title: Common atmospheric pollutants and their sources
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Common atmospheric pollutants and their sources — AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification, section 4.9.3.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering Common atmospheric pollutants and their sources, specification section 4.9.3.
final_note: You worked through Common atmospheric pollutants and their sources — 11 specification statements.

concepts.def: The burning of a fuel in oxygen, releasing energy. The combustion of fuels is a major source of atmospheric pollutants.
A substance released into the atmosphere that harms human health or the environment. Burning fuels is a major source of such substances.
Most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may also contain some sulfur. The elements present in the fuel decide which pollutants its combustion can release.
Burning in a plentiful supply of air, so that the carbon in the fuel is oxidised to carbon dioxide and the hydrogen is oxidised to water, released as water vapour.
Burning in a limited supply of air, so that some carbon is only partly oxidised to carbon monoxide or is released as solid carbon (soot), and some hydrocarbon may pass through unburned.
A gas, formula CO, produced when a carbon-containing fuel burns in a limited supply of air so that the carbon is not fully oxidised.
Solid particles of carbon released when a fuel burns in a limited supply of air. Soot and unburned hydrocarbons form particulates in the atmosphere.
Tiny solid particles suspended in the atmosphere, formed from solid particles such as soot and from unburned hydrocarbons released when fuels burn.
A gas, formula SO2, produced when sulfur present as an impurity in a fuel is oxidised as the fuel burns.
Gases formed when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react together at the high temperatures reached inside an engine or a furnace. The nitrogen comes from the air, not from the fuel.
The gaseous water released when the hydrogen in a fuel is oxidised during burning. It is one of the gases released into the atmosphere when a fuel is burned.
A gas that poisons the body. Carbon monoxide is a toxic gas, and because it is colourless and odourless it is not easily detected.
Rain made acidic by pollutants dissolving in it. Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause acid rain.
Damage to or irritation of the breathing system in humans. Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems in humans.
The reduction in the amount of sunlight reaching the Earth's surface caused by particulates in the atmosphere. Particulates also cause health problems for humans.

mcqs.q: A monitoring station in a city records carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and particulates in the air above a busy road. What do these three pollutants have in common?
options: All three are released when fuels are burned
All three form from nitrogen in the air
All three come from sulfur in the fuel
All three are solid bits of unburnt fuel
mcqs.explain: The specification names the combustion of fuels as a major source of atmospheric pollutants, and all three of these are released when fuels burn.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes what most fuels, including coal, contain?
options: Carbon and/or hydrogen, and always a little sulfur
Carbon and/or hydrogen, and possibly some sulfur
Carbon and nitrogen, and possibly some sulfur
Sulfur and oxygen, and possibly some carbon
mcqs.explain: This is what the specification states: most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may also contain some sulfur.

mcqs.q: A hydrocarbon fuel burns completely in a plentiful supply of air. Which two substances are released?
options: Carbon monoxide and water vapour
Sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide and water vapour
Carbon dioxide and hydrogen
mcqs.explain: With plenty of air the carbon is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide and the hydrogen is oxidised to water, released as water vapour.

mcqs.q: Solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons are released from a burning fuel. What do they form in the atmosphere?
options: A gas called carbon monoxide
Sulfur dioxide in the air
Acid rain that harms lakes
Particulates in the air
mcqs.explain: The specification states that solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons form particulates in the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: Petrol is burned inside a car engine and carbon monoxide is found in the exhaust gases. Why is carbon monoxide produced?
options: Nitrogen from the air combines with carbon atoms
The oxygen supply is limited, so combustion is incomplete
Sulfur in the petrol takes oxygen from the carbon
The oxygen supply is plentiful, so carbon burns fully
mcqs.explain: Inside the engine the air supply is limited, so some carbon is only partly oxidised and carbon monoxide forms instead of carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: Oxides of nitrogen are found in the exhaust gases of a hot car engine. Where does the nitrogen in them come from?
options: From nitrogen compounds present inside the fuel
From sulfur impurities reacting with hot air
From nitrogen in the air drawn into the engine
From nitrogen given off as the fuel breaks up
mcqs.explain: Air is about four-fifths nitrogen, and at the high temperature inside the engine that nitrogen reacts with oxygen from the air.

mcqs.q: A fuel contains carbon, hydrogen and a small amount of sulfur. It is burned in a plentiful supply of air. Which products are formed?
options: Carbon dioxide, hydrogen and sulfur dioxide
Carbon monoxide, water and sulfur dioxide
Carbon dioxide, soot and sulfur dioxide
Carbon dioxide, water and sulfur dioxide
mcqs.explain: With plenty of air the carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide, the hydrogen to water, and the sulfur impurity to sulfur dioxide.

mcqs.q: A gas heater burns methane in a room where the air vent has been blocked, so the oxygen supply is poor. Which product now appears that would not be formed with plenty of air?
options: Carbon monoxide
Nitrogen dioxide
Unburned hydrogen
Sulfur dioxide gas
mcqs.explain: With a limited oxygen supply the carbon in the methane is only partly oxidised, so carbon monoxide is formed instead of carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: Carbon monoxide leaks from a faulty boiler into a house. Why is this so dangerous?
options: It has a sharp smell that people learn to ignore
It turns the water vapour in the room into acid
It is toxic, and colourless and odourless so hard to spot
It is explosive and can set the whole room alight
mcqs.explain: The specification states that carbon monoxide is a toxic gas and that it is colourless and odourless, so it is not easily detected.

mcqs.q: Which pollutants does the specification name as the causes of acid rain?
options: Carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide
Particulates and oxides of nitrogen
Carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons
Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
mcqs.explain: The specification states that sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems in humans and cause acid rain.

mcqs.q: As well as causing acid rain, sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen affect people directly. What effect on humans does the specification give?
options: They cause problems with breathing
They cause dimming of sunlight
They make a hole in the ozone layer
They cause skin damage from sunlight
mcqs.explain: The specification states that sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems in humans.

mcqs.q: Particulates in the atmosphere cause health problems for humans. What other effect does the specification give for particulates?
options: They add to global warming
They cause global dimming
They cause acid rain damage
They destroy the ozone layer
mcqs.explain: The specification states that particulates cause global dimming and health problems for humans.

mcqs.q: Particulate levels in the air over a city rise year after year, and less sunlight now reaches the streets. Why do particulates have this effect?
options: They are suspended solids that block sunlight
They are a gas that soaks up light and heat
They trap warmth near the Earth's surface
They have thinned the ozone layer above us
mcqs.explain: Particulates are tiny solids suspended in the air. They reflect and absorb sunlight on its way in, so less reaches the surface: global dimming.

mcqs.q: Stonework on a city building is being eaten away, and tests show the rain falling there is acidic. Which rise in air pollution explains this damage?
options: More sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
More carbon dioxide from the burning fuel
More carbon monoxide from car exhausts
More particulates from sooty chimneys
mcqs.explain: The specification gives sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen as the causes of acid rain, which is what attacks the stonework.

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.9.3 Common atmospheric pollutants and their sources
